name: Question 3
problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2},\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{2},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*
worked_solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{4}}{4}-(\frac{(-\pi )^{4}}{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }-{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }-{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-(-(-\pi )\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )))+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\pi +\pi +(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =2\pi \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Question 3
?

Consider the following set of functions: f1(t)=t,f2(t)=t2,f3(t)=sin⁡t

Given that the inner product in the vector space C[−π,π] of continuous functions over [−π,π] is defined as ⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=∫−ππf(t)g(t)dt, which of the following statements are true?

  1. f1(t)⊥f2(t) with respect to the given inner product
  2. f1(t)⊥f3(t) with respect to the given inner product
  3. S={f1(t),f2(t),f3(t)} is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
Hint: ⟨f2,f3⟩=0.

a
None of the statements are true
b
I and III only
c
I, II, and III
d
II only
e
I only
Don't Know

EXPLANATION

Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. We have ⟨f1(t),f2(t)⟩=⟨t,t2⟩=∫−ππt⋅t2dt=∫−ππt3dt=t44|−ππ=π44−((−π)44)=0. This means that f1(t)⊥f2(t) with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is false. We have ⟨f1(t),f3(t)⟩=⟨t,sin⁡t⟩=∫−ππtsin⁡tdt. Let's use integration by parts. We denote u=t⟹u′=1,v′=sin⁡t⟹v=∫v′dt=∫sin⁡tdt=−cos⁡t. Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain ∫−ππtsin⁡tdt=uv|−ππ−∫−ππu′vdt=(−tcos⁡t)|−ππ−∫−ππ(−cos⁡t)dt=(−π⋅cos⁡(π)−(−(−π)⋅cos⁡(−π)))+sin⁡t|−ππ=π+π+(sin⁡(π)−sin⁡(−π))=2π≠0. This means that f1(t)⊥̸f3(t) with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Since f1(t)⊥̸f3(t), the set S is not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
